title: The Great Cedar Confusion
subtitle: Why none of New England's "cedars" are real cedars

content.text: If you've ever heard of "Eastern Red Cedar" or "Atlantic White Cedar" or "Northern White Cedar" and assumed they were all related — you're not alone. But here's the twist: none of these trees are actually cedars.

content.heading: What's a "Real" Cedar?
content.text: True cedars belong to the genus Cedrus and are native to the Mediterranean and Himalayas. They include the Cedar of Lebanon, Atlas Cedar, and Deodar Cedar. These are the trees that gave us the word "cedar" — and none of them grow wild in New England.

content.heading: Eastern Red Cedar — Actually a Juniper
content.text: Juniperus virginiana is our most common "cedar." It's actually a juniper — the same genus that gives us juniper berries (used to flavor gin). You can tell by its blue-gray berry-like cones and its two types of leaves: sharp juvenile needles and flat, scale-like adult leaves. It thrives in abandoned fields and along fence rows.

content.heading: Atlantic White Cedar — A False Cypress
content.text: Chamaecyparis thyoides belongs to the false cypress genus. Found in swampy, boggy areas along the coast, it has tiny scale-like leaves pressed flat against its branchlets. Its wood is famously rot-resistant, which is why early colonists used it for shingles, boats, and fence posts.

content.heading: Northern White Cedar — An Arborvitae
content.text: Thuja occidentalis is an arborvitae (meaning "tree of life" — it reportedly saved Jacques Cartier's crew from scurvy in 1536). It has flat, fan-like sprays of scale leaves and is often planted as a hedge. In the wild, it loves wet, limy soils and rocky shorelines.

content.heading: Why the Confusion?
content.text: Early European settlers in North America encountered aromatic, rot-resistant softwoods and called them "cedar" because they reminded them of the cedars they knew from the Old World. The name stuck, even though these trees are in completely different genera and even different families.

Quick way to remember: If a tree is called "cedar" in New England, it's NOT a true cedar. Eastern Red Cedar = juniper. White Cedar = either arborvitae or false cypress. True cedars (Cedrus) are only found in gardens and parks here.

title: Hemlock the Tree vs. Hemlock the Poison
subtitle: Two completely unrelated things that share a confusing name

content.text: When you hear "hemlock" you might think of Socrates and his famous poisoning. But the Eastern Hemlock tree you'll find throughout New England's forests is completely harmless — and completely unrelated to the poison.

content.heading: The Tree: Eastern Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis)
content.text: Eastern Hemlock is a beautiful, shade-tolerant evergreen conifer in the pine family. It has short, flat needles with two white stripes underneath and tiny oval cones. It's one of the most important trees in New England's forests, creating cool, shady ravines that support unique ecosystems. You can even make tea from its needles — they're rich in vitamin C.

content.heading: The Poison: Poison Hemlock (Conium maculatum)
content.text: Poison hemlock is a flowering plant in the carrot family (Apiaceae) — the same family as parsley, carrots, and Queen Anne's lace. It's a tall herb with white umbrella-shaped flower clusters and purple-spotted hollow stems. This is the plant that killed Socrates. It contains coniine, a powerful neurotoxin.

content.heading: Why the Same Name?
content.text: The tree got its name because its crushed needles supposedly smell similar to the poison hemlock plant. European settlers who encountered the tree used the familiar name from back home. The two organisms are about as distantly related as any two plants can be — one is a conifer, the other a flowering herb.

Bottom line: Hemlock trees are safe. They're big, evergreen conifers with needles and cones. Poison hemlock is a weedy herb with white flowers and spotted stems. If it has needles, it's the tree — and it's harmless.

title: New England's Three Conifer Families
subtitle: A quick guide to telling pine family, cypress family, and yew family apart

content.text: All of New England's conifers belong to just three families. Once you can tell these three apart, you've already narrowed down any conifer you find to a small group.

content.heading: Pine Family (Pinaceae) — 24 Species
content.text: This is the big one. It includes pines, spruces, firs, hemlocks, larches, and Douglas-fir. The key feature: they all have needles (not scales) and their cones have woody scales arranged in a spiral. Pine needles come in bundles of 2, 3, or 5. Spruce needles are sharp and square in cross-section. Fir needles are flat and soft. Hemlock needles are short with white stripes underneath.

content.heading: Cypress Family (Cupressaceae) — 7 Species
content.text: This family includes junipers, arborvitae, Atlantic white cedar, baldcypress, and dawn redwood. Most members have tiny scale-like leaves pressed flat against their branchlets (not needles). Junipers are the exception — they can have both sharp needles and scales. Their cones are often small and berry-like (especially in junipers) rather than the classic woody pine cone shape.

content.heading: Yew Family (Taxaceae) — 3 Species
content.text: Yews are the oddball conifers. They have flat, dark green needles arranged in two rows along the stem — somewhat similar to hemlock but wider and darker. Instead of cones, they produce bright red berry-like structures called arils. Important: yew seeds and foliage are toxic to humans and animals. The red aril flesh itself is not toxic, but the seed inside is.
Three-step conifer ID: (1) Scale-like leaves? → Cypress family. (2) Red berry-like fruits? → Yew family. (3) Needles with woody cones? → Pine family.
